title: Enrollment ‘Fraud Ring’ Forces Some Grossmont-Cuyamaca Online Classes to In-Person Instruction
summary: Emails show a purported enrollment fraud ring is plaguing the Grossmont-Cuyamaca Community College District. In response, officials have partnered with law enforcement agencies and moved some online classes to in-person instruction. The post Enrollment ‘Fraud Ring’ Forces Some Grossmont-Cuyamaca Online Classes to In-Person Instruction appeared first on Voice of San Diego .
content: In response to an alleged enrollment fraud ring at the Grossmont-Cuyamaca Community College District, officials are moving many online classes at one of the district’s colleges to in-person instruction. The fraud ring has also reportedly spurred an investigation from local and federal law enforcement, though it’s unclear which agencies have taken the lead. “It is with grave concern that we inform you that our colleges have been targeted by a financial aid fraud ring impacting hundreds of students enrolled in online classes,” Grossmont-Cuyamaca Chancellor Lynn Neault wrote in a Nov. 5 email to faculty . The news is just the latest in an ever-evolving string of enrollment fraud at community college districts nationwide. Post-pandemic, the trend hit a fever pitch, as more colleges have turned to online courses and generative AI has allowed students to submit fake work. The trend usually looks like this : fraudsters steal identities, enroll in community colleges that accept all comers and then submit fake work to reap financial aid dollars. That’s not exactly what’s being alleged at Grossmont-Cuyamaca, though. Leadership at the district first made faculty aware of the alleged ring in a Nov. 5 email. In the email, Neault wrote the “fraud ring” was not composed of bots, a colloquial term used to refer to networks of fraudulent students that have bilked financial aid funds at other community colleges. Instead, these were “individuals residing in our community.” Staff had discovered the fraudulent activity earlier this year and had begun to take steps to combat it, largely by placing enrollment holds on students they knew to be fraudulent. Still, faculty should “be on high alert for suspicious patterns,” like AI-generated assignments and similar errors between student assignments. Neault also advised that they not respond to inquiries from students with enrollment holds as “the inquiries may or may not be from the actual students.” “This is an active investigation,” Neault wrote. “We will continue to report all suspicious activity to law enforcement and fully cooperate to ensure the criminals are prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” In response to a series of questions from Voice of San Diego, Grossmont-Cuyamaca spokesperson Sara Spiva wrote, “To protect the integrity of an ongoing investigation, the Grossmont-Cuyamaca Community College District is unable to comment or provide further information at this time.” Cuyamaca Shifting to In-Person Classes While fraudulent activity is happening at both of the district’s colleges, it appears to be focused primarily on Cuyamaca College, a small community college in the southern corner of El Cajon. “For this reason, our response has been swift, including moving online courses with high levels of identified fraudulent enrollment to in-person instruction for spring 2027,” Cuyamaca College President Jessica Robinson wrote in a Nov. 18 email to staff. Robinson didn’t say how many online classes were impacted by fraudulent activity in her email. But beginning in fall 2027, Cuyamaca plans to default to in-person instruction over online for all classes at the college. Online or hybrid courses will be offered to support student access as needed but will have to be approved by the college dean and vice presidents. “I know these changes bring real concerns about student access, full-time faculty reaching load, assignments for our part-time colleagues, and enrollment overall,” Robinson said. “We do expect a decline in enrollment as fraudulent enrollments are removed and schedules change.” That decline in enrollment presents real risks for Cuyamaca. A district report shows that in fall 2025, 57 percent of classes students enrolled in were delivered online. Should a portion of students choose not to re-enroll in person, it would be a serious hit for the small community college. The fraud concerns may also put in danger the college’s ability to receive federal financial aid for some of its online courses. In the email, Robinson wrote that the situation “adds to the complexity of our accreditation work on regular and substantive interaction in distance education.” That accreditation stems from Department of Education regulations that require colleges’ online courses to meet certain benchmarks to qualify fully as providers of “distance education.” Those benchmarks include direct instruction, student engagement and regular assignments. If an institution does not meet those benchmarks, they may be subjected to an audit or be ruled ineligible to receive financial aid. Grossmont Keeping Online Courses Unlike Cuyamaca, Grossmont officials don’t have plans to change how they deliver online courses for the spring 2027 semester or next fall, Interim President Pamela Luster wrote in an email to staff on Nov. 19 . Grossmont College is tucked into the foothills bordering Mission Trails in northwestern El Cajon. According to the district’s enrollment report, 47 percent of Grossmont’s student population took online classes last fall. Instead of completely removing the option for students, Luster said that the college plans to closely monitor and adjust online courses as needed. In the meantime, Luster asked that faculty report any “unusual patterns” from students to the district, and to monitor student participation, updating their rosters as needed to “protect the integrity of our enrollment and financial aid processes.” “We cannot lose sight of the fact that the overwhelming majority of our students are here to learn, improve their lives, and achieve their goals,” she said. “We also have a responsibility to protect the integrity of our college, our programs, and the public resources entrusted to us.” The post Enrollment ‘Fraud Ring’ Forces Some Grossmont-Cuyamaca Online Classes to In-Person Instruction appeared first on Voice of San Diego .

title: Beef Week: Encinitas and Former Mayor at Odds Again
summary: Former Encinitas mayor and now state Sen. Catherine Blakespear is once again at odds with her hometown. This isn’t necessarily new, but the beef between Blakespear and a lot of […] The post Beef Week: Encinitas and Former Mayor at Odds Again appeared first on Voice of San Diego .
content: Former Encinitas mayor and now state Sen. Catherine Blakespear is once again at odds with her hometown. This isn’t necessarily new, but the beef between Blakespear and a lot of the city’s residents and public officials has escalated since the last time we wrote about it . And this time, there’s a lawsuit involved. Blakespear has come under fire for recently adding a provision to a state bill that specifically doesn’t allow Encinitas to remove or modify protected bike lanes on Santa Fe Drive. That didn’t go over well with city leaders who were actively working on doing just that. So now, they’re suing the state. Our Tigist Layne previously wrote about the lingering resentment from many residents toward Blakespear because of her stint as mayor, which was a total of six years concluding in 2022 when voters elected her to the state Senate District 38. Blakespear has said it’s because her time as mayor was so “active,” meaning she accomplished a lot. She led the city to adopt its first state approved Housing Element in almost two decades, she advocated for North County’s first safe parking lot to open in Encinitas and more, feats that earned her plenty of fans and a lot of haters. This time, though, the beef is going to court. Read the latest full story in our Beef Week series here. Fraud Ring Forces Community College to Shift Many Online Classes to In Person Earlier this month, Grossmont-Cuyamaca Community College District leaders announced their two colleges were being targeted by a financial aid and enrollment fraud ring. A couple weeks later, officials at Cuyamaca Community College told staff they’ll be shifting many online classes to in-person instruction starting in 2027. Grossmont officials plan on keeping their classes as is, while closely monitoring them and making changes as needed. Cuyamaca College, a small community college in El Cajon, was hit the hardest, prompting officials to shift the online classes being targeted the most, even though it could hurt the college long term, both financially and with its enrollment numbers. Unfortunately, the district is only the latest victim in a string of community college districts nationwide that have experienced similar attacks, especially with the rise of generative AI. Unlike many other incidents, though, this fraud ring seems to be made up of individuals in the community rather than bots, according to district officials. Read the full story here. Found in the Scroll: El Niño Brings Rare Sea Creatures to SoCal Different marine species exotic to the California coast have been showing up in San Diego lately due to El Niño. Last week, there were several rare sightings of the Portuguese man-o’-war, which is usually found near Hawaii and Australia. Now, fishermen are seeing the dolphinfish around the LA area, which can grow up to 6 feet and weigh up to 90 lbs. In Other News San Diego Unified will pay $2.4 million to settle lawsuits from two administrators who accused former superintendent Lamont Jackson of sexually harassing them, and then retaliating against them when they rejected his advances. (Union-Tribune) A young man has filed a lawsuit against the city of San Diego because a police officer allegedly shot him while he was on his way to work. (Times of San Diego) Hollywood can’t get enough of San Diego. A new movie starring Chris Pratt was filmed throughout San Diego , including at the airport and Mission Bay. (Union-Tribune) The National Weather Service office in San Diego is reminding residents to stay safe this week as they expect powerful waves will hit beaches and coastal communities. (NBC 7) The Morning Report was written by Tigist Layne and Andrea Sanchez-Villafaña. It was edited by Andrea Sanchez-Villafaña. title: The Ongoing Feud Between Encinitas and Catherine Blakespear
summary: The beef between the former mayor and her hometown now involves a lawsuit. The post The Ongoing Feud Between Encinitas and Catherine Blakespear appeared first on Voice of San Diego .
content: It’s been four years since state Sen. Catherine Blakespear concluded her time as mayor of Encinitas, but in some ways it’s like she never left. She led the city for six years before voters elected her to the state Senate District 38 in 2022, where she still represents the North County city. Now, she’s at odds with the city after she added a provision in a state bill that essentially forces city leaders to keep any existing bike lanes. It’s the latest flashpoint in a long-running tension between the former mayor and her hometown. Voice of San Diego previously reported about that many residents and elected officials trace their frustrations about housing, homelessness and infrastructure back to Blakespear’s time as mayor. Too much high-density development springing up around town? That’s in part because when Blakespear led the effort to get the city’s Housing Element, or housing plan, approved with the state several years ago, she was too lenient with the building standards she committed the city to, outgoing Encinitas Mayor Bruce Ehlers previously told Voice . Seeing a year-over-year increase in street homelessness? Some residents blame Blakespear’s approval of bringing North County’s first safe parking lot to Encinitas a few years back, arguing it drew homeless people into the city from other parts of the county. Blakespear is once again the subject of residents’ vitriol. This time, she’s at the center of an ongoing dispute about bike lanes that has escalated into Encinitas suing the state. Beef Week is a Voice of San Diego reporting series. This week our newsroom will bringing you stories about all the beef and battles in San Diego. Read more Beef Week stories here. In September, she added a last-minute provision to a recently approved state law that restricts Encinitas from further changing the very controversial Santa Fe Drive project, a bike lane and roadway improvement project on a stretch of Santa Fe Drive south of San Dieguito Academy. The previous City Council implemented the project using more than $3 million in state funding secured by Blakespear. It narrowed car lanes to 10 feet, added angled back-in parking and installed separated bike lanes, along with pedestrian improvements and other measures to calm traffic. The city has a tragic history with traffic incidents related to cyclists and pedestrians, so, bike and pedestrian safety is often one of residents’ top priorities. Construction concluded in April 2025. Seven months later, the current City Council voted to make plans to undo and change a lot of it. They want to remove the back-in parking spots — which seem to be very unpopular — widen the vehicle lanes and replace one of the protected bike lanes with a traditional edge-of-roadway bike lane. A second protected bike lane would remain as is. The changes are expected to cost more than $3 million. The project and the plan to redo it has gotten a lot of attention, including from Blakespear. She had previously said she wouldn’t interfere in any of the changes as long as the protected bicycle lanes remained, but that if the Council planned to remove any of them, she would get involved. In June, Blakespear used a legislative process known as “gut and amend” to change SB 569, a bill about homeless encampments, into a bill focused on bike lane infrastructure. It said that infrastructure separating bike lanes from traffic can’t be removed without a public review overseen by a licensed engineer and an evaluation of safety and connectivity. She told the Coast News it was prompted in part by Santa Fe Drive but in general wanted to ensure that removing bike lanes faced the same scrutiny as installing them. The bill drew a lot of backlash, with critics calling it an overreach by the state into local infrastructure decisions. Proponents said it would prevent bike lanes from being removed simply because of things like changes in political leadership or public opinion. Ultimately, the bill reached the Assembly floor but was moved to the inactive file and never received a final vote. But Blakespear didn’t give up there. Weeks later, in the final days of the legislative session, she added a provision to SB 114, a larger state budget bill. It prohibits Encinitas, specifically, from “removing or modifying” separated bike lanes on Santa Fe Drive for five years after the project’s completion. Between five and 15 years, the city can remove the protected bike lane, but only if the removal “results in equal or greater safety, accessibility and mobility for non-motorized users,” it says . If Encinitas leaders move forward with their plans anyway, they would have to repay the $3.09 million in state grant funds that Blakespear secured for the project in 2023. Now, city leaders are suing. At a recent North County mayors forum at Pacific Ridge School in Carlsbad, Ehlers said the provision is “probably illegal” because SB 114 is a fiscal bill and Blakespear’s provision doesn’t have a fiscal component. He called the matter “far from over.” BTW Ehlers just lost his re-election campaign for mayor to Democrat Rimga Viskanta, so we’ll see how this all shakes out. Encinitas has a history of brush ups with the state, although, they’ve typically been over housing laws. Past City Councils have received multiple warnings over the years from Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office, State Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office and the state housing department about their failure to adopt a Housing Element and multiple violations of state housing laws. But those past incidents never escalated to the state suing Encinitas, let alone the other way around. “The budget provision enacted to prohibit the removal of a state-funded, barrier-protected bike lane that makes it safer for cyclists to be on the street in Encinitas is logical, reasonable and completely legal,” Blakespear told Voice via email. “The lawsuit filed by the city of Encinitas against this provision is a performative, waste of time that will be thrown out by the court.” Blakespear is very aware of the reputation she has among a portion of residents; it’s difficult to tell if it’s a large portion or just a more outspoken one. Nonetheless, she hears it all, and she doesn’t seem to let it shake her. “The way I see it is my time at City Hall was so active, and we did so much, and I’m a convenient scapegoat for the problems and inconveniences that people see in modern life,” she told Voice back in January.
